text:
Published: September 25, 2026

NEW YORK, USA — Liberia warns that a rapid global transition away from fossil fuels in international shipping could drive up freight and commodity costs, worsen food insecurity, and place severe economic pressure on African and other developing countries unless the International Maritime Organization carefully considers the consequences before implementing its Net-Zero Framework.

By Blamo N. Toe

Liberia’s Permanent Representative to the International Maritime Organization, Robert Kpadeh, sounded the warning Thursday during a special interview with OK TV in New York, USA, where Liberian officials have been making the case for what they describe as a more just and equitable pathway toward reducing emissions from global shipping.

Kpadeh stressed that Liberia is not opposing the IMO’s efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions or the broader transition toward cleaner alternative fuels. Instead, he said the country is pushing for comprehensive economic impact studies and a phased approach that accounts for the heavy dependence of African countries, least developed countries and small island developing states on maritime trade.

“What Liberia is saying is that this cannot be a quick-fix decision. This cannot be an abrupt decision. It has to be studied properly,” Kpadeh said.

He argued that moving too quickly, without fully determining the availability, affordability, and commercial viability of alternative fuels, could have consequences extending far beyond the shipping industry.

For Liberia, Kpadeh said, the stakes are particularly high because the country depends heavily on ships for rice, petroleum and other essential commodities while also deriving significant economic benefits from its international ship registry.

“Everything we do in Liberia, from rice to petroleum to commodities, comes into our country,” he said. “So, we are a shipping country.”

Kpadeh warned that higher shipping and freight costs could eventually reach ordinary citizens through increased commodity prices and greater pressure on food security, while weakening governments’ ability to invest in schools, roads, health care and other essential infrastructure.

He said Liberia is therefore urging IMO member states to ensure that efforts to confront climate change do not create another economic crisis for countries already struggling with development challenges.

“You want to balance the transition,” Kpadeh said. “You want to be sensitive to reducing the threat of climate change, but also you don’t want to do it at the expense of poor countries, at the expense of developing countries, at the expense of struggling people.”

Liberia is instead advocating a step-by-step transition that Kpadeh said could still achieve the international community’s emissions-reduction objectives without unnecessarily disrupting economies heavily dependent on maritime trade.

“We can still get to what we want to get to,” he said, “but we cannot just rush there.”

text:
The energy sector is developing zero-emission bunker fuel supply and infrastructure to meet the IMO’s 2030 target of 5-10% uptake. But vessel orders and commercial demand are struggling to keep pace.

IMAGE: G2 Ocean's Star Lygra cargo ship carrying Amazon's containers. X of @Port_Houston 2

The IMO wants zero- or near-zero-emission energy to account for at least 5% of international shipping’s energy consumption by 2030, striving for 10%.

But the shipping industry still has a long way to go to meet this ambition, probably even further than two years ago.

In September 2024, researchers at the UCL Energy Institute and the Getting to Zero Coalition, run by the Global Maritime Forum (GMF), found that fuel supply was partially on track but demand was lagging. Two years later, their September 2026 report suggests little has changed.

“In several cases, progress has not only slowed relative to previous years but regressed,” the 2026 report said.

The assessment focuses on e-methanol and e-ammonia as scalable zero-emission fuels (SZEF) with a well-to-wake GHG intensity below 19 gCO2e/MJ. It excludes e-methane because of its methane slip, as well as blue fuels produced from fossil feedstocks with carbon capture and storage.

The report said production of SZEF still has the potential to catch up by 2030, but weakening demand from shipowners and cargo owners risks leaving that potential untapped.

More ships, but where’s the demand?

DNV data shows that five ammonia-capable vessels are now in operation, up from two in September 2024, with another 41 on order for delivery by 2030, compared with 28 two years ago.

The operational methanol- and ethanol-capable fleet has roughly tripled from 53 to 160 vessels over the same period, but its orderbook has barely moved from 294 to 299.

"The 2024 shift away from conventional fuels thus appears to have been a one-off pulse driven by a few large operators rather than a structural break in ordering behaviour," the GMF and UCL report noted.

But more fuel-capable vessels do not necessarily translate into higher green fuel consumption. The GMF and UCL report's authors found that actual SZEF consumption on dual-fuel ships remains "negligible".

Based on the current fleet and orderbook, vessels would have the capacity to consume only around 12 million mt/year of e-methanol and e-ammonia by 2030, measured in heavy fuel oil-equivalent. This falls short of the 15 million mt/year minimum needed to meet the IMO’s 5% target.

Cargo owners tighten purse strings

The other side of the demand equation doesn’t look much better.

A Boston Consulting Group (BCG) survey of 125 cargo owners, published in April, found that the average green premium they were willing to pay fell to 3% in 2025 from 4.5% in 2024. The share of respondents prepared to pay more than 20% extra for low-emission fuels dropped to zero from 3% over the same period.

Only 45% expected to be willing to pay a premium within the next five years, down from 65% in 2024.

High fuel costs relative to their commercial benefits were the most frequently cited barrier, combined with wider regulatory and economic uncertainty.

But waning willingness to pay does not mean all cargo owners have stopped paying for emissions reductions. Some are paying a premium for emissions reductions through book-and-claim arrangements, even if their own cargo travels on a conventionally fuelled vessel. These arrangements could help create demand for e-fuels.

For instance, DP World will use Hapag-Lloyd's biofuel-based service to claim around 4,700 mtCO2e of emissions reductions. Gap will use Maersk's biofuel- or bio-methanol-based service to purchase reductions for its European trade lanes.

Pooling demand offers another route.

The Zero Emission Maritime Buyers Alliance (ZEMBA) pools demand from cargo owners including Amazon, DSV, Google and Microsoft. Its second tender will support Hapag-Lloyd's planned e-methanol deployment and North Sea Container Line's e-ammonia-powered service.

Together, the shipping companies are expected to cut GHG emissions by around 120,000 mtCO2e over three years from 2027, with ZEMBA members purchasing the reductions through book-and-claim.

How ready is ready?

Shipowners are also keeping their fuel options open. Fuel-ready tonnage accounts for 2.48% of the active fleet, against just 0.77% already SZEF-capable, the GMF and UCL report's authors found.

Höegh Autoliners recently ordered six LNG dual-fuel car carriers with notations for future conversion to ammonia and methanol, without specifying their level of readiness.

But fuel-ready does not mean fuel-capable. Höegh’s vessels will run on LNG or conventional fuels until converted. Other fuel-ready ships may continue using conventional fuels. Shipowners could also choose not to convert them at all.

And until the conversion takes place, these vessels cannot use the intended zero-emission fuels.

"The failure to adopt the NZF [Net-Zero Framework] was the single most transition-regressive event we've seen in the five years this report has been running," said Pinar Langer, research fellow at the UCL Energy Institute.

Regulatory certainty this year is what it will take to win back vessel orders and investment, Langer argued. The IMO's next chance to adopt the Net-Zero Framework comes in December.

In other alt fuels news this week, US President Donald Trump has signalled that his administration intends to prevent the IMO from adopting a global emissions-pricing mechanism. "There is no global government - and while I am President, there will be no global taxes," he said.

Class society American Bureau of Shipping has granted approval in principle to the design of a 22,000-cbm ammonia bunker vessel.

Singapore-based global shipping company Eastern Pacific Shipping has taken delivery of an LPG dual-fuel very large ammonia carrier from China's Jiangnan Shipyard.

However, Liberian representatives emphasized that ambitious climate action must advance alongside sustainable development, particularly for developing economies that rely heavily on international maritime trade.
To prevent these outcomes, Liberia is calling for economic realities to remain central to international maritime climate policymaking alongside environmental objectives.

text:
By Amos Harris

Liberia is intensifying its advocacy for a fair, practical, and equitable approach to decarbonizing international shipping, warning that the global transition to net-zero emissions must not create new economic burdens for developing nations.

The Liberian Government outlined its stance during a high-level engagement with United Nations Member States, where it presented an alternative proposal to the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) Net-Zero Framework.

As a leading flag state and a climate-vulnerable developing nation with deep historical and economic ties to the sea, Liberia reaffirmed its full support for global efforts to combat climate change and reduce greenhouse gas emissions from maritime transport. However, Liberian representatives emphasized that ambitious climate action must advance alongside sustainable development, particularly for developing economies that rely heavily on international maritime trade.

Liberia’s proposed framework advocates for a maritime transition that is pragmatic, realistic, performance-based, affordable, scalable, equitable, and legally coherent within the IMO’s existing mandate.

The government expressed serious concern over the potential fallout of steeply rising maritime transportation costs, noting that shipping is essential for importing food, fuel, medicine, machinery, construction materials, and other vital commodities. Liberian officials warned that inflated shipping rates could trigger broader economic distress across developing countries, including elevated food and energy prices, persistent inflation, eroded trade competitiveness, and derailed development goals.

To prevent these outcomes, Liberia is calling for economic realities to remain central to international maritime climate policymaking alongside environmental objectives. The proposal urges the IMO to conduct country-specific economic impact assessments, recognizing that developing nations possess distinct economic structures, trade patterns, technological capacities, infrastructure levels, financing access, and maritime dependencies.

Rather than imposing punitive costs, Liberia’s strategy promotes commercially viable alternative fuels, enhanced operational efficiency, technological innovation, infrastructure expansion, and targeted capacity-building as the most viable pathways toward sustainable shipping. The government stressed that financial and technical support mechanisms for developing nations must be predictable, transparent, equitable, and directly responsive to local needs.

Liberia maintains that instead of forcing developing nations to absorb major financial shocks before receiving aid, the Net-Zero Framework should be engineered from the outset to prevent disproportionate economic harm. The country also championed evidence-based decision-making, urging the IMO to rigorously evaluate the technical credibility, legal consistency, affordability, administrative feasibility, and scalable availability of proposed green fuels and measures.

Officials stressed that Liberia’s position is not aimed at weakening global climate ambitions, but at ensuring climate action and economic development move forward in tandem. Liberia reiterated that the long-term effectiveness and legitimacy of the IMO depend on fostering trust and meaningful participation among all Member States—including developed and developing nations, flag states, and coastal states alike.

“Net zero must not become a new burden on developing countries,” the Liberian position underscores, emphasizing that the global transition should instead open avenues for sustainable investment, innovation, technology transfer, infrastructure upgrades, and capacity development.

Liberia reaffirmed its commitment to collaborating constructively with IMO Member States and international stakeholders to shape a maritime decarbonization framework that effectively combats climate change while safeguarding global trade, food security, and economic resilience.

The IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) is scheduled to continue high-level deliberations on the Net-Zero Framework at its next session in November 2026. Liberia plans to remain actively engaged in pre-session consultations and negotiations to secure an outcome that is environmentally ambitious, economically sound, and equitable for all nations.

text:
Regulatory uncertainty is becoming a major factor in shipowners’ investment decisions as the industry weighs vessels and fuel systems that will remain in service for decades, according to DNV’s latest Maritime Forecast to 2050.

The report examines four possible regulatory futures, ranging from full adoption of the International Maritime Organization’s Net-Zero Framework to outright rejection and prolonged political gridlock. Between those extremes are scenarios involving a delayed or revised framework and a greater role for regional regulations.

The uncertainty comes as the IMO prepares to return to the Net-Zero Framework in October, one year after governments adjourned the extraordinary Marine Environment Protection Committee meeting without adopting the regulations.

DNV said the eventual outcome could significantly change the economics of alternative fuels, energy-efficiency investments and fleet renewal.

“Decisions taken today on vessel design, retrofits, and fuel capability will determine competitiveness for decades, while the outcome of ongoing regulatory negotiations could significantly reshape the economics of shipping’s energy transition,” said Øyvind Sekkesæter, senior consultant at DNV and lead author of the report.

Under stronger global regulation, DNV estimates the world fleet could consume as much as 25% less energy by 2050 compared with a scenario driven primarily by regional rules. Demand for low-greenhouse-gas fuels could also vary widely depending on the regulatory path, ranging from 33 million tonnes of oil equivalent to 185 million tonnes by 2050.

The wide range underscores one of the report’s main conclusions: shipowners may have less reason to bet on a single future fuel than to build flexibility into their fleets.

That is already visible in the orderbook. DNV said alternative-fuel-capable tonnage has grown from just 0.4% of the global fleet in 2020 to 5.2% in 2026, led by LNG and methanol systems. But many dual-fuel vessels continue operating primarily on conventional fuels because alternatives remain more expensive and incentives for switching remain limited.

Energy efficiency presents a more straightforward investment case.

DNV modeled a retrofit of a hypothetical 15-year-old, 5,000-TEU containership involving a new bow, propeller upgrade and propeller boss cap fin at a cost of $2.35 million. The measures produced estimated fuel savings of about 16%, with payback periods ranging from 1.4 to 4.2 years depending on fuel prices.

The net present value of the savings could reach between $2 million and $10 million by 2038, even before accounting for compliance costs under the European Union Emissions Trading System and FuelEU Maritime.

“The key takeaway from this study is that even a 15-year-old vessel can offer a compelling business case for retrofitting energy-saving measures,” Sekkesæter said. “Unlike fuel choices, efficiency improvements create value under every regulatory scenario.”

DNV also pointed to real-world performance data showing the potential value of relatively simple maintenance measures. On one chartered vessel, hull and propeller cleaning reduced its Vessel Technical Index from an average of 1.32 to 1.14, with 1.00 representing an “as-new” baseline.

The improvement saved roughly 120 tonnes of fuel during a 33-day voyage. At $470 per tonne, the savings totaled about $56,000, compared with a cleaning cost of $14,000.

Fuel availability remains another major constraint.

The LNG bunkering fleet has expanded from 25 vessels in 2020 to 67 today, while 24 methanol bunkering vessels are operating and another eight are on order. But supplies of genuinely low-GHG fuels remain concentrated in Europe and East Asia.

DNV found that low-GHG fuels have been bunkered at nearly 90 ports worldwide, though availability differs sharply by fuel. Biodiesel is available at nearly 70 ports, liquefied biomethane at 20 and low-GHG methanol at 16. Low-GHG ammonia has so far been bunkered at only three ports, all in East Asia.

Shipping will also have to compete with aviation, manufacturing, power generation and road transport for many of the same fuels and feedstocks. DNV estimates demand across all sectors could exceed 2.2 billion tonnes of oil equivalent under a global net-zero pathway, increasing pressure on supplies of biofuels and potentially forcing greater reliance on more expensive e-fuels and blue fuels.

The result, DNV argues, is an increasingly difficult investment environment in which flexibility may carry its own value.

“Shipowners need fuel and technology strategies that remain competitive across different regulatory outcomes,” Sekkesæter said. “At the same time, clear demand signals and concerted efforts are needed to scale the solutions and infrastructure supporting shipping’s energy transition.”

DNV released the 10th edition of its Maritime Forecast to 2050 in late August. The report is intended to help owners evaluate fuel, technology and efficiency investments against multiple possible regulatory outcomes rather than relying on a single decarbonization pathway.

title: Trump Renews Attack on IMO Net-Zero Shipping Framework at UN General Assembly
description:
🇬🇷 Διαβάστε στα Ελληνικά President Donald Trump used his address to the United Nations General Assembly to renew his attack on the International Maritime Organization’s Net-Zero Framework, accusing the UN shipping agency of attempting to impose a global carbon tax that would drive up transportation costs.
“Last year, my administration was forced to intervene to stop an obscure U.N. body, the International Maritime Organization, from secretly establishing a first-ever global carbon tax,” Trump said, claiming the measure would raise international shipping costs by “10 to 20% — and maybe more than that.” He added, “There is no global government,” and “while I’m president, there will be no global taxes.” The remarks elevate a fight that has been playing out at the IMO for more than a year and come as member states prepare for another attempt to finalize the framework in December.
The Trump administration played a major role in last year’s decision to postpone adoption, with U.S. officials threatening countries supporting the framework with measures including tariffs, visa restrictions, port fees and sanctions ahead of the vote, which the extraordinary Marine Environment Protection Committee session ultimately postponed for one year following a 57-49 tally.
The proposed mechanism, which supporters call a greenhouse-gas pricing system tied to ships’ emissions performance rather than a tax, could generate an estimated $10 billion to $15 billion annually to fund cleaner marine fuel development, though opponents including the U.S. and several oil-producing nations continue to raise concerns over its economic impact.

title: World Maritime Day 2026: IMO Warns Shipping Rules Are Under Strain as Seafarers Face ...
description:
The International Maritime Organization has chosen “From Policy to Practice: Powering Maritime Excellence” as the World Maritime Day theme for both 2026 and 2027, putting the focus on whether international shipping rules are actually being implemented and enforced at the national level.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres said this year’s observance comes as the international maritime framework itself faces growing pressure.
“With at least 80 per cent of international trade moving by sea, maritime shipping keeps our world afloat,” Guterres said.
For the first time, the World Maritime Day theme will span two years, giving governments and industry through 2027 to focus on moving regulations from adoption to implementation.
This year’s World Maritime Day Parallel Event will be held in Busan, South Korea, on October 26-27.
text:
The global maritime industry is marking World Maritime Day on Thursday with an unusually immediate backdrop: merchant ships under attack, seafarers being killed and some of the world’s most important shipping routes disrupted by conflict.

The International Maritime Organization has chosen “From Policy to Practice: Powering Maritime Excellence” as the World Maritime Day theme for both 2026 and 2027, putting the focus on whether international shipping rules are actually being implemented and enforced at the national level.

The message comes as commercial shipping continues to face the effects of geopolitical conflict from the Strait of Hormuz to the Black Sea and Sea of Azov. IMO said attacks on merchant ships have killed dozens of seafarers while disrupting trade and critical supply chains.

“This year’s World Maritime Day theme, ‘From Policy to Practice: Powering Maritime Excellence’, recognizes the reality that regulations will deliver safer, more resilient, and cleaner shipping when they are implemented worldwide,” IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez said.

“Implementation must make a difference where it matters most — for the people working at sea. Seafarers come first. Always.”

The theme reflects a longstanding challenge for the IMO. The organization develops global rules covering ship safety, environmental protection, security and other areas, but those rules ultimately depend on individual governments to incorporate them into national law and enforce them.

IMO this year completed the first audit cycle under the mandatory IMO Member State Audit Scheme, which assesses how effectively countries meet their obligations under key IMO instruments. Since mandatory audits began in February 2016, 168 audits covering 165 Member States and three Associate Members have been carried out.

The results exposed persistent gaps. IMO said some countries continue to struggle to translate international rules into domestic law, with shortages of technical expertise and infrastructure as well as weak oversight of ships among the key problems. The organization plans to use the findings to better target technical assistance, including support for Least Developed Countries and Small Island Developing States.

That assistance includes help drafting national legislation, building maritime administrative and enforcement capacity, and training regulators, port officials and seafarers.

The two-year World Maritime Day theme will also extend across some of the biggest issues currently confronting shipping, including new technologies, decarbonization, fraudulent ship registration, digitalization, cyber and maritime security, and marine environmental protection.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres said this year’s observance comes as the international maritime framework itself faces growing pressure.

“With at least 80 per cent of international trade moving by sea, maritime shipping keeps our world afloat,” Guterres said.

“But this critical framework is under strain. Conflicts and geopolitical tensions are infringing on navigational rights and freedoms that must be restored. The lives of seafarers are being threatened, and the global supply of fuel, fertilizers and food has been disrupted.”

He said governments, labor groups and industry all have a role in translating international commitments into practical improvements, from worker safety to shipping’s energy transition.

The International Chamber of Shipping also voiced support for the IMO’s World Maritime Day message, saying it “stands with and strongly supports” the organization as it marks this year’s theme.

For the first time, the World Maritime Day theme will span two years, giving governments and industry through 2027 to focus on moving regulations from adoption to implementation. IMO says the longer timeframe is intended to emphasize technical assistance, training and capacity building rather than simply the development of new rules.

IMO headquarters in London will be illuminated in blue Thursday evening, with Member States and maritime organizations invited to do the same as a symbol of the international commitment to safe, secure and resilient shipping.

This year’s World Maritime Day Parallel Event will be held in Busan, South Korea, on October 26-27.

text:
The energy transition of maritime transport is shaping around different fuel alternatives and technologies, with no single solution applicable to the entire global fleet at this time. The strategies published by A.P. Moller-Maersk and Mitsui O.S.K. Lines (MOL) reflect this scenario, with programs considering different fuels based on their availability, the characteristics of the vessels, and the evolution of international regulations.

This approach aligns with the conclusions of the fifth edition of the report Climate Action in Shipping: Progress towards Shipping’s 2030 Breakthrough, produced by UCL Energy Institute and Getting to Zero Coalition and presented this week during Climate Week in New York. The study assesses the progress toward the goal that between 5% and 10% of the fuel used by international maritime transport in 2030 comes from scalable zero-emission sources.

Maersk currently maintains an approach based on a portfolio of different fuels. In 2025, it incorporated ten new container ships powered by dual methanol propulsion, signed a supply agreement for liquefied biomethane —bio-LNG— and conducted tests with e-methanol blends. The company believes that diversifying propulsion options will allow it to gradually adapt its fleet to the availability of fuels with lower emissions.

This strategy had already been reflected in the fleet renewal program announced by the shipping company, which includes dual systems of methanol and liquefied gas. Maersk then indicated that it anticipates a future with different fuels and that the choice of technologies will depend, among other factors, on the regulatory framework and the availability of fuels with lower emissions. The company also maintains a favorable position towards a technologically neutral international regulatory framework that encourages the development of scalable zero-emission fuels.

MOL follows a similarly diversified strategy. The update of its Environmental Vision – BLUE ACTION 2035 Phase 2, published in April 2026, considers the use of LNG and biodiesel in the short and medium term, and a subsequent transition towards bio-LNG, e-LNG, and other alternatives. According to the company's documentation, in March of this year, it had 112 vessels capable of using LNG, including 87 methanol carriers and 25 units from other segments.

The Japanese shipping company is also developing projects related to methanol and ammonia. In February, it participated in the first ship-to-ship methanol supply operation carried out at anchor in Yokohama, and in June, signed long-term charter contracts with JERA for two large vessels intended for low-carbon ammonia transport. MOL states in its corporate documentation that it will continue to work with a combination of biofuels, methanol, ammonia, and hydrogen, in addition to expanding the use of bio-LNG.

The report presented in New York situates these business decisions within a scenario where technology and supply are showing progress, although other indicators evolve more slowly. The number of ports offering methanol supply increased from 19 to 29 during the last year, while the operational tonnage ready to use methanol grew from 2.3 to 7.7 million GT. The proportion of the active fleet compatible with scalable zero-emission fuels rose from 0.41% to 0.77%.

The evolution of the order book, however, presents a different trend. Vessels prepared to use this type of fuel reduced their weight from 9.5% to 5.7% of the contracted tonnage, while the report estimates a potential demand for scalable zero-emission fuels of about 0.45 exajoules in 2030, compared to the 0.6 EJ associated with the minimum threshold of 5%.

The study also identifies a reduction in signals from cargo owners. The declared willingness to pay a premium for maritime services with lower emissions fell from 4.5% to 3%, while the proportion of shippers expecting to bear a higher cost over the next five years dropped from 65% to 45%.

UCL Energy Institute and Getting to Zero Coalition classify the areas of technology and supply and civil society participation as partially on track, while they consider that demand, financing, and regulation are outside the expected trajectory. The report links part of this situation to the uncertainty generated after the adoption of the International Maritime Organization's Net-Zero Framework was postponed to October 2025.

text:
NEW YORK — Liberia is lobbying governments to remove the carbon price and global fund from the International Maritime Organization's net-zero shipping rules before they reconsider adoption. The Liberian team argues that the framework, in its current form, would raise the cost of food, fertilizer, and exports for developing countries that trade with distant markets.

Liberian maritime officials made the case Wednesday at a side event on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly, alongside Foreign Minister Sara Beysolow Nyanti. They presented an alternative co-sponsored by Panama, which the team calls a pragmatic and performance-based path to the IMO's goal of net-zero emissions from shipping by 2050.

"The issue that we want to address today is not whether we support climate ambition. It is rather whether the IMO proposed measures are fair, practical and connected to real emissions reductions," said Cllr. Margaret C. Ansumana, deputy commissioner of the Liberia Maritime Authority, who introduced the proposal.

The IMO's Marine Environment Protection Committee approved the Net-Zero Framework in April 2025. It would require large ships to meet annual fuel-intensity targets or cover excess emissions with credits bought from other ships or payments into a new IMO Net-Zero Fund. An extraordinary session convened to adopt it in October 2025 instead voted 57 to 49 to adjourn for one year, with 21 abstentions. Reports put adoption later this year, around October or November.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Liberia's plan would keep a global fuel standard but tie it to fuels that are commercially viable, meaning available, affordable and scalable across all regions, rather than setting it on climate ambition alone. The standard would be reviewed every five years against emissions progress, the impact on developing economies and the maturity of clean fuels.

Ships that beat the standard would earn surplus units they could transfer within a fleet to vessels that fall short. Ships on routes where clean fuel is not available could also earn units for verified energy-efficiency measures, such as slowing down to burn less fuel.

The proposal removes the penalty payments that ships unable to find compliant fuel or surplus units would owe under the current framework. A member of the Liberian technical team, Ms. Grace Nuhn said charging ships for a fuel they cannot get amounts to letting them pay and keep polluting.

"It's like you're telling someone that depends on rice to stop eating rice, and the alternative you are providing is not available to them," said Ms. Nuhn, a technical presenter on the Liberian team. "Rules are made to help people."

The Liberian team argued that shipowners would not absorb compliance costs and would pass them to consumers. They said countries that import food and fertilizer and export raw materials over long distances would pay the most.

The deputy commissioner Asumana said the framework in its current form is projected to raise about US$10 billion to US$12 billion a year. She called that money a compliance cost that developing economies would ultimately bear, and said it was unclear how much of it would return to them.

A technical officer on the Liberian team said Liberia's own impact assessment covered only one export, iron ore. The officer said adding rice, the country's staple, and other goods moved by ship would paint a worse picture. The team urged other least developed countries and small island developing states to run their own country-level assessments rather than rely on regional studies.

The team said the plan would still meet the IMO's 2023 greenhouse gas strategy. The presenter said it would cut emissions by 25% by 2030, above the strategy's 20% target, while striving for 30%. By 2040 it would reach about 75%, within the strategy's range of 70% to 80%, and net zero by 2050, as cleaner fuels mature and the standard tightens.

The Liberian officials also said MARPOL, the international convention on pollution from ships, should remain a technical instrument. They said it should not carry a financing mechanism such as the Net-Zero Fund.

Liberia Maritime Authority Commissioner Neto Zarzar Lighe Sr. said the question for poor and island nations is whether they should first bear heavy trade and economic costs to raise money that may never fully offset the harm.

"Our objective is not to weaken ambition, but to make it achievable, equitable, and sustainable for all member states, especially developing and climate vulnerable countries," Lighe said.

He described the New York event as a continuation of a presentation the team made in London a few weeks earlier. He thanked Panama for co-sponsoring the proposal.

Minister Nyanti said the Foreign Ministry's role is to mobilize international support for Liberia's agenda on maritime safety, maritime security and its net-zero program as part of the country's climate diplomacy. She said the ministry fully aligns itself with the position of Liberia's maritime experts. She said discussions on net zero would take place at several high-level meetings and side meetings next month.

Liberia's Permanent Reprsentative to the United Nations, Amb. Lewis Brown, who closed the event, said Liberia is the largest ship registry by tonnage, which brings climate responsibility. He said Liberia does not want to penalize countries that are not the main polluters, "nor do we wish to permit people who can pay for pollution to simply pay for it and get away with it."

Several Middle Eastern and North African states supported Liberia's proposal during IMO talks in April, among them Oman, Kuwait, Jordan, Somalia, Yemen and Tunisia. The president of the Union of Greek Shipowners, Melina Travlos, endorsed it in August.

Liberia, Argentina and Panama had all opposed the framework before sponsoring the alternative. The United States led opposition to the framework when it was presented in 2025.

text:
Target-setting remains under discussion

The IMO’s recent ISWG-GHG 22 discussions provided greater clarity on the remaining design questions around the proposed Net-Zero Framework, although Member States reached no final decisions. The working group examined target-setting, compliance mechanisms, financing for a just and equitable transition, and incentives for zero and near-zero emission (ZNZ) fuels.

The Center for Zero Carbon Shipping, which attended an IMO meeting for the first time as an accredited NGO with consultative status, said discussions showed “forward momentum” despite several issues remaining unresolved.

However, according to MMMCZCS, one key question is whether the NZF should establish emissions-reduction targets in advance to drive the development and uptake of low-emission fuels, or whether targets should instead reflect the commercial availability of such fuels.

Liberia has proposed linking targets to commercial viability, using criteria including fuel price, market share and availability at ports. Japan has proposed a hybrid approach, with fixed targets through 2035 and later targets determined following reviews of commercial viability.

Member States also discussed the stringency of the targets. Brazil and Japan have proposed softer trajectories through 2035/2036 compared with the draft framework approved at MEPC 83. Brazil’s proposal would ultimately reach a 70% base target reduction in 2041, compared with the draft NZF’s 65% target for 2040.

Another unresolved issue is whether to establish a long-term target beyond 2035/2036. The draft NZF and proposals from Brazil and Tuvalu include targets for 2040/2041, while Japan proposes leaving the longer-term target to a 2032 review of commercial viability.

The Center said it intervened during the meeting to support long-term targets, arguing that they can provide certainty for investment and encourage industry-led innovation.

This was an important meeting. The mood was constructive, and it felt like there was good engagement and discussion of some key issues. While little was definitively settled, there is definitely forward momentum.

… said Fiona McIlwham, Head of Public Affairs & Strategic Communication.

Compliance options

Member States broadly agreed that reducing emissions should remain the primary compliance mechanism for ships. There was also broad acceptance of allowing emissions credits to be traded between ships, including the use of surplus units to meet both Tier 1 and Tier 2 targets.

However, questions remain over whether ships should be able to comply through remedial units or similar financial mechanisms.

Under the draft NZF, Tier 2 remedial units would initially cost $380/tCO2eq, while Tier 1 units would cost $100/tCO2eq and generate revenues intended to support a just and equitable transition and ZNZ fuels.

Some delegations argued that such mechanisms could weaken incentives to reduce emissions, while others viewed them as necessary flexibility if surplus compliance units become scarce.

Financing a just and equitable transition

Member States reaffirmed support for a just and equitable transition, but remain divided over how financial support should be generated and administered.

Concerns have been raised about the governance, administrative costs and institutional mandate of an IMO-managed Net-Zero Fund. Liberia and Panama have proposed removing mandatory revenue generation and relying on voluntary support.

Alternative models discussed include Brazil’s proposed facility, potentially hosted by an international financial institution; Japan’s direct voluntary contribution scheme, under which shipping companies would select eligible projects; and Canada’s proposal for a roster of eligible funds meeting criteria established by the IMO.

Incentives for zero and near-zero emission fuels

There was broad support for retaining a dedicated incentive for ZNZ fuels, although the mechanism remains undecided.

China has proposed both a fixed monetary reward and a calculation-based multiplier. Under the multiplier concept, ZNZ energy receives additional weight in the attained GFI calculation, increasing a ship’s compliance surplus.

China’s indicative multiplier would decline from about 1.95 in 2029 to 1.10 in 2035, reflecting an expected reduction in the cost gap between conventional marine fuels and ZNZ alternatives.

The Center noted that a multiplier could provide an automatic incentive without relying on revenue collection and distribution, but could also increase the supply of surplus units and affect their market value.

MEPC 85 to address remaining questions

The remaining issues will be discussed at another ISWG-GHG meeting beginning 23 November 2026, followed by MEPC 85 from 30 November to 4 December 2026.

Member States could approve a revised draft amendment at that stage, although further postponement remains possible. If the required six-month circulation period has been completed, the IMO could also move towards adoption, with 4 December set aside for a possible resumption of the extraordinary session.

If the amendments are not ready for adoption, the decision could instead be deferred to MEPC 86, expected in October 2027.

text:
The shipping industry faces a growing risk of failing to meet its 2030 zero-emission fuel targets, largely because of regulatory uncertainty over the past year, according to a new report from the Global Maritime Forum.

Read also: Port Electrification Could Cut 10% of Shipping Emissions

The fifth edition of the Climate action in shipping: Progress towards shipping’s 2030 breakthrough report, launched during New York Climate Week, measures how far the sector has moved toward its goal of sourcing at least 5 to 10 percent of the fuel used in international shipping from scalable zero-emission sources by 2030. That range represents the estimated uptake needed to satisfy the 2023 International Maritime Organization Greenhouse Gas Strategy and, ultimately, the industry’s 2050 net-zero objective.

Mixed progress across five levers

The report assesses the sector through five levers: technology and supply, demand, finance, policy, and civil society. It describes achievements over the past year alongside stagnation or decline in other areas.

Among the gains, the period saw the first ammonia bunkering and sea trials worldwide. The number of ports offering methanol bunkering rose 53 percent, from 19 to 29. Methanol-capable in-service tonnage tripled, the largest single-year capability increase on record. Shipping finance portfolios also recorded their greatest improvement in climate alignment to date.

Jesse Fahnestock, director of decarbonisation at the Global Maritime Forum, said the energy transition is necessary and will happen, pointing to worsening climate impacts. He noted that the 2030 breakthrough target was embraced by an industry that must bring tomorrow’s zero-emission fuels to market today. While geopolitical turmoil over the past year has frustrated the process, he said accelerated industry action could still deliver on the ambition with the right policy push, and that adoption of the Net-Zero Framework at the IMO would allow that acceleration to begin.

Dan Ioschpe, Climate High-Level Champion for COP30, said the pathway to zero remains achievable, investable, and aligned with development goals. He described progress in technology and zero-emission fuel supply as encouraging but said investment decisions cannot wait, adding that demand for zero-emission shipping and financial flows toward it are critical to accelerating the pace. Done properly, he said, climate action in shipping would increase competitiveness, improve energy security, and drive socio-economic development.

Demand, finance and policy lag

Despite the positive developments, the report finds that other key levers, particularly demand, finance, and policy, have either stagnated or worsened since the previous edition. Demand signals weakened amid a widespread wait-and-see approach to global regulation. The order book regressed, with scalable zero-emission fuel-capable vessels falling from 9.5 percent to 5.7 percent of total tonnage on order. Shipping-specific sustainable debt issuance declined from 3.4 billion dollars in 2024 to 3.0 billion dollars in 2025.

Dr Pinar Langer, a research fellow at the UCL Energy Institute, described the failure to adopt the Net-Zero Framework as the single most transition-regressive event in the five years the report has run. She said reversing that momentum loss and securing regulatory certainty this year is among the most important next steps to give shipowners confidence to order zero-emission vessels, lenders incentive to invest in them, and charterers impetus to pay for low-carbon shipping.

Recommendations and tracker

The report recommends that the IMO adopt the Net-Zero Framework as is at its upcoming session in December, which it says would create the global policy clarity and direction the ecosystem urgently needs. It also stresses the growing importance of national and regional policies that underpin scalable zero-emission fuel production to de-risk first-mover action, regardless of what happens next at the IMO.

The 2026 progress tracker rates technology and scalable zero-emission fuel supply as partially on track, demand as not on track, finance as not on track, policy as not on track, and civil society as partially on track.

The report sets conditions for what qualifies as scalable zero-emission fuel. Such fuels must be scalable enough to match current annual consumption of 200 to 300 million tonnes of oil equivalent in the foreseeable future, producible with greenhouse gas intensity reductions of 90 to 100 percent relative to incumbent fossil-based fuels on a full life cycle well-to-wake basis, and competitive in production cost in the foreseeable future assuming continued research and development and viable policy support mechanisms. The definition excludes biofuels, less-polluting fossil fuels including liquefied natural gas, blue fuels derived from fossil fuel sources such as hydrogen produced from natural gas, and applications of carbon capture. Options not at a high technology readiness level and facing significant adoption barriers are also excluded.

The NZF includes a global fuel standard and an economic mechanism designed to price greenhouse gas emissions from international shipping.

text:
Launched on September 18, the Hub is intended to provide a single source of information on emerging low carbon liquid fuel technologies, supply chains, sustainability considerations and opportunities for Australia. The initiative comes as demand for alternatives to conventional fossil fuels grows across sectors including transport and shipping.

The Hub was delivered in partnership with Queensland University of Technology through the iMOVE Cooperative Research Centre. The Australian Government contributed A$162,500 toward the initiative.

Low carbon liquid fuels can be used as alternatives to conventional diesel, jet fuel, petrol and marine fuels. According to the Australian Government, these fuels can be produced from biomass and waste materials, including agricultural and forestry by-products, as well as from renewable hydrogen combined with captured carbon dioxide.

It is worth noting that the Australian Maritime Safety Authority (AMSA), in its report“New Build Trends in Australia’s Domestic Fleet 2023–2024,” identified the adoption of alternative fuels as an emerging trend, pointing to the domestic fleet’s gradual shift toward lower-carbon operations.

The Australian Government said the Hub will bring together information covering the development and deployment of these fuels, helping users better understand their potential applications as well as the challenges associated with their production and supply.

Relevance for maritime fuel transition

The development comes as shipping faces a rapidly changing alternative-fuel landscape, with shipowners, ports and fuel suppliers examining a combination of options to reduce emissions.

Liquid fuels are expected to remain important to shipping because they can potentially be stored, transported and bunkered using infrastructure and operational systems that are more familiar to the industry than some alternative energy carriers.

However, their environmental performance depends heavily on how they are produced. Biofuels, for example, can have substantially different lifecycle emissions depending on the feedstock and production pathway, while synthetic fuels can offer different emissions profiles depending on the source of electricity, hydrogen and carbon.

For this reason, information on feedstocks, certification and lifecycle emissions is becoming increasingly important alongside the technical availability of alternative fuels.

The Australian Hub brings these issues together in one resource, with the government describing the initiative as a means of making emerging fuel technologies and their associated supply chains easier to understand.

Australia’s development of the Hub also reflects the wider shift toward establishing domestic knowledge and supply-chain capacity for low carbon fuels, as industries prepare for tighter emissions requirements and growing demand for lower-carbon energy.

text:
US President Donald Trump has signalled that his administration intends to prevent the IMO from adopting a global emissions-pricing mechanism.

IMAGE: US President Donald Trump addressing the UN General Assembly on 22 September. The White House

"Last year, my administration was forced to intervene to stop an obscure UN body, the International Maritime Organization, from secretly establishing a first-ever global carbon tax, very expensive tax, to raise international shipping costs by 10-20% and maybe more than that," Trump said while addressing the UN General Assembly on 22 September.

"There is no global government - and while I am President, there will be no global taxes," he added.

The US delegation walked out of negotiations at the IMO's 83rd Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 83) meeting in April 2025. The meeting ended with a draft Net-Zero Framework (NZF) being approved by 63 votes to 16, with 24 abstentions.

The draft NZF introduced a two-tiered GHG fuel standard that would require ships to progressively reduce their well-to-wake GHG fuel intensity (GFI) from 2028.

Ships that fall short of the direct compliance target would be required to purchase remedial units to cover their emissions deficit through contributions to the IMO Net-Zero Fund. The Tier 1 remedial unit price is set at $100/mtCO2e for 2028-2030.

Those that fail to meet both the base and direct compliance targets would also need to cover an additional Tier 2 deficit. This could be done by purchasing surplus units from other ships, using units banked from previous years or buying additional remedial units at a higher price of $380/mtCO2e for 2028-2030.

However, formal adoption of the NZF was postponed for one year in October 2025 amid vocal opposition from the US and several other oil-producing countries.

Ahead of MEPC 84 in April, Washington called for an “energy-all” approach in its own submission to the IMO, arguing that proposals should not restrict use of conventional crude or diesel, LNG, nuclear power, biomass-based fuels or other marine propulsion technologies.

It also supported a separate position put forward by Algeria, Bahrain, Iraq, Kuwait, Russia, Saudi Arabia, Somalia and the UAE, which warned that a framework containing economic measures would not secure consensus.

At MEPC 84, the US then joined Liberia, Panama and Argentina in pushing for negotiations on their proposal to remove GHG pricing and revise the GFI reduction trajectory, the US State Department said.

Despite the opposition, 59 member states at MEPC 84 supported using the approved NZF as the basis for the draft terms of reference guiding further discussions at the IMO’s GHG working group meetings in September and November, according to the UCL Energy Institute.

The outcome of those negotiations will be considered at MEPC 85, scheduled between 30 November-3 December. If a final text is agreed, the framework could then be adopted at the resumed second extraordinary session (MEPC/ES.2) on 4 December, subject to confirmation by MEPC 85.

US backs nuclear propulsion

The Trump administration is also working with the UK government to explore nuclear-powered commercial shipping, including the potential for a transatlantic corridor.

More recently, A.P. Moller - Maersk joined Lloyd’s Register and the ports of Charleston, US and Felixstowe, UK, to model operational and regulatory requirements for such a corridor under the bilateral initiative.

text:
Speaking at the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on September 22, Trump singled out the IMO when discussing his administration’s opposition to what he described as international taxation and regulation.

Last year, my administration was forced to intervene to stop an obscure U.N. body, the International Maritime Organization, from secretly establishing a first ever global carbon tax

… Trump said. He claimed the measure could raise international shipping costs by 10% to 20%, “and maybe even more than that.”

IMO Net-Zero Framework

The comments relate to the IMO’s Net-Zero Framework, which member states approved in draft form at MEPC 83 in April 2025. The framework combines a mandatory global marine fuel standard with a global economic mechanism intended to price greenhouse gas emissions from international shipping.

There is no global government. And while I’m president, there will be no global taxes

… Trump stressed

Under the framework approved in 2025, ships of more than 5,000 GT, accounting for about 85% of CO2 emissions from international shipping, would be subject to progressively stricter greenhouse gas fuel-intensity requirements.

Ships exceeding the applicable emissions thresholds would need to obtain remedial units, while ships meeting more ambitious standards could generate surplus units. Contributions to the proposed IMO Net-Zero Fund would also support low-emission shipping, research and development, infrastructure and a just transition in developing countries.

The IMO has characterized the mechanism as a global greenhouse gas emissions pricing system rather than a conventional tax. It is designed to create an economic incentive to reduce emissions while generating funding for the transition to zero- and near-zero-emission fuels and technologies.

Adoption was postponed

The framework was originally scheduled for formal adoption in October 2025. However, member states agreed to postpone the decision for one year following an extraordinary session of the Marine Environment Protection Committee.

The postponement followed intense opposition from the United States and other countries. The decision was adopted by 57 votes to 49, with the framework’s formal adoption deferred for a year.

The issue therefore remains unresolved as the IMO prepares for the next phase of negotiations in 2026.

The U.S. administration has continued to oppose the proposed economic mechanism. During the April 2026 IMO negotiations, Washington circulated material arguing that the proposed carbon pricing system could impose significant additional costs on international trade.

Shipping costs and competitiveness at the center of debate

Trump’s UNGA remarks place the potential cost implications of the framework at the center of the U.S. position.

The economic mechanism is intended to increase the cost of higher-emission fuels and create financial incentives for ships using zero- or near-zero-emission alternatives. The IMO has also proposed using revenues to support developing countries and vulnerable states affected by the transition.

The framework has nevertheless generated debate over how the costs would ultimately be distributed across shipowners, cargo interests and consumers, particularly in developing and trade-dependent economies.

The dispute comes as shipping continues to face several overlapping regulatory costs. In Europe, for example, international shipping is already subject to the EU Emissions Trading System, while FuelEU Maritime has introduced greenhouse gas intensity requirements for ships calling at EU ports.

Wider implications for global shipping

Trump’s intervention also highlights the increasingly political dimension of shipping’s decarbonization agenda.

The IMO’s 2023 GHG Strategy established the objective of reaching net-zero GHG emissions from international shipping by or around 2050, with interim targets for 2030 and 2040. The Net-Zero Framework is intended to translate those ambitions into mandatory requirements applicable across the international fleet.

At the same time, shipping’s regulatory environment is becoming increasingly fragmented, with regional measures developing alongside the IMO’s global framework. The outcome of the negotiations over the Net-Zero Framework will therefore have implications not only for vessel compliance and fuel choices, but also for the future structure of international shipping’s emissions regulation.

Trump’s intervention comes as the U.S. administration is also pressing for changes to the role of international organizations and has criticized what it considers excessive authority being exercised by UN bodies. His UNGA speech presented the IMO framework as an example of what Washington regards as an unacceptable global regulatory or taxation mechanism.

Meanwhile, maritime organizations and other stakeholders continue to emphasize the importance of maintaining a common international regulatory framework for shipping, particularly as the sector faces the practical challenge of decarbonizing a globally traded fleet.

text:
The World Maritime Day is approaching, set for September 24. This is a particularly significant date in the maritime transport sector, which the International Maritime Organization (IMO) will celebrate under the theme “From Policy to Practice: Driving Maritime Excellence.” This theme will be maintained for two years to highlight the mission of this global body in ensuring a global regulatory framework and promoting a safe, efficient, and environmentally sustainable sector that operates according to international standards and continuously strives for improvement.

In the context of this upcoming celebration, Trasmed, the Spanish shipping company of the Grimaldi Group, has asserted the role of the IMO as a global reference for the regulation of maritime transport. This is a framework in which this global organization has been working for over 70 years through international maritime agreements.

Both the Spanish shipping company and much of the sector advocate prioritizing the IMO's guidelines over the proliferation of local, regional, national, and supranational regulations. As Miguel Pardo, Trasmed's Director of Public Relations, points out, “the maritime transport activity is a global business that is complicated to regulate locally without generating distortions to competition.”

IMO's Commitment to Activate the SDGs

In addition to valuing the role of the IMO as a guarantor of international maritime law, this global organization aims to strengthen its support for the 2030 Agenda and the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) set, especially those that most impact the maritime transport sector, such as: SDG 9 on industry, innovation, and infrastructure, SDG 13 related to climate action, SDG 14 related to life below water, and SDG 17 on partnerships.

Trasmed adds, in this regard, the importance of contributing to goals such as SDG 8, Decent Work and Economic Growth, or SDG 11, Sustainable Cities and Communities, in which maritime transport plays a relevant role as connectors of territories and people, contributing to a more cohesive and prosperous society, as the Spanish shipping company advocates.

text:
Both this year and next, the International Maritime Organization is focusing its World Maritime Day message on an issue of growing concern: getting its hard-won regulations into use on the waterfront, everywhere that ships go. It's not enough to pass a convention, even one as useful as SOLAS - each IMO rule also has to be implemented in each member state. That means translating the convention into national law, then training up officials to put it into practice, then using it for enforcement. The degree of compliance varies, and while IMO can't police its member states, it can help them to get better.

Since 2016, IMO has implemented a mandatory audit scheme (IMSAS) to check up on how well its members are complying with IMO instruments. So far, 168 member states - all but a handful - have been audited. The results, according to IMO, are revealing.

IMO's advisory teams have found that "many countries still struggle to translate IMO rules into national law, with shortage of technical expertise and infrastructure, and weak oversight of ships." In response, the IMO allocates its technical assistance resources to places that need the most help, places that include least developed countries and small island developing states. As some of these member states operate well-known open flag registries, a local-level improvement in compliance could translate into global improvement in shipping safety.

text:
OMV Petrom has confirmed major construction progress on its new sustainable fuels unit at the Petrobrazi refinery in Romania.

The €560 million project will create a 250,000‑tonne‑per‑year facility producing SAF and renewable diesel (HVO) from vegetable oils and used cooking oil, supported by green hydrogen. Foundations are complete and key process equipment — including columns and reactors up to 60 metres high—has been installed.

The flexible unit will be able to switch product slate between SAF, HVO, bio‑naphtha and bio‑LPG depending on market demand and feedstock availability, delivering at least 65% lifecycle CO₂ reductions versus fossil fuels.

Commissioning is targeted for 2028, alongside new electrolyser capacity for green hydrogen at Petrobrazi.

OMV Petrom positions the project as a cornerstone in transforming the refinery into a regional hub for low‑carbon fuels serving aviation and heavy transport.

“Petrobrazi is going through one of the most important transformations in its recent history. With a €560 million investment, we are building a new unit that will produce 250,000 tonnes per year of sustainable fuels made from renewable feedstocks.

“These lower carbon fuels will contribute to reducing emissions in sectors where electrification is difficult, such as aviation and heavy transport.

“We have completed the foundations, for which approximately 20,000 cubic meters of concrete were poured, and equipment up to 60 meters high is already installed in the refinery.

“This is a project through which we are gradually adapting Petrobrazi to the new requirements of the market and of the energy transition, including through the development of sustainable fuels production,” said Radu Căprău, member of the OMV Petrom Executive Board.

text:
The International Maritime Organization has marked World Maritime Day on 24 September with a push for governments to turn global shipping rules into national legislation and stronger enforcement, according to a statement.

The 2026 event is being held under the theme “From Policy to Practice: Powering Maritime Excellence”, which will remain in place through 2027. It is the first time the UN shipping agency has adopted a World Maritime Day theme for a two-year period.

IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez, a Panamanian naval architect and former Panama ambassador to IMO, said implementation of international regulation must deliver practical results for people working at sea.

“Implementation must make a difference where it matters most - for the people working at sea. Seafarers come first. Always,” Dominguez said.

The agency said implementation requires governments to translate IMO regulations into domestic legislation, strengthen enforcement and improve training. Its focus includes safety and new technologies, shipping decarbonisation, fraudulent ship registration and maritime fraud, digitalisation and resilience, cyber security, maritime security and protection of the marine environment.

The initiative follows completion of the first cycle of the IMO Member State Audit Scheme in June. Mandatory audits began in 2016, with 168 audits conducted across 165 Member States and three Associate Members.

The audits identified recurring shortcomings in national legislation, enforcement, technical expertise and implementation. IMO plans to use the findings to target technical assistance and capacity building.

IMO headquarters in London will be illuminated in blue on 24 September. A World Maritime Day Parallel Event will be held in Busan, South Korea, on 26 and 27 October.

IMO is the UN specialised agency responsible for international shipping safety and security and prevention of pollution from ships. It has 176 Member States and three Associate Members. Dominguez became its 10th Secretary-General on 1 January 2024.

text:
Shipping is at greater risk of missing its 2030 zero-emission fuel target following a year of regulatory uncertainty, according to a new report.

The 2026 edition of Climate Action in Shipping: Progress Towards Shipping’s 2030 Breakthrough report published by the Global Maritime Forum and UCL Energy Institute under the Getting to Zero Coalition on Tuesday, tracks the industry’s progress towards its 2030 climate targets.

It assesses progress towards having 5-10% of international shipping’ marine fuel come from scalable zero-emission fuels (SZEF) by 2030, a level considered important for putting the sector on a pathway towards net-zero emissions by 2050.

The report said the failure to adopt the IMO Net-Zero Framework last year was the “single most transition-regressive event” recorded during its five-year history.

Progress has nevertheless continued in some areas.

The number of ports offering methanol bunkering rose 53% year-on-year from 19 to 29, while methanol-capable in-service tonnage tripled.

The past year also saw the first ammonia bunkering operation and sea trials, while shipping finance recorded its strongest improvement in climate alignment on record.

However, the share of SZEF-capable vessels in the orderbook fell from 9.5% to 5.7%, while sustainable debt issuance declined from $3.4 billion in 2024 to $3 billion in 2025.

The report called for the IMO to adopt the Net-Zero Framework at its December session to restore regulatory certainty.

text:
US President Donald Trump has renewed his opposition to the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) Net-Zero Framework, accusing the UN shipping agency of seeking to impose a global carbon tax that would increase shipping costs.

Addressing the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, Trump said his administration had previously intervened to block what he described as the IMO’s attempt to establish a “first-ever global carbon tax”.

He claimed the measure could increase international shipping costs by 10 to 20 per cent or more.

“There is no global government,” Trump said. “And while I’m president, there will be no global taxes.”

The remarks come as IMO member states prepare to resume negotiations ahead of a potential December vote on the framework, which would introduce tighter greenhouse-gas intensity requirements for marine fuels alongside an economic mechanism for ships with higher emissions.

The Trump administration played a key role in last year’s decision to postpone adoption, including threatening countries backing the framework with possible tariffs, visa restrictions, port fees and sanctions.

While Washington describes the proposed mechanism as a global carbon tax, supporters refer to it as a greenhouse-gas pricing system linked to ships’ emissions performance.

The proposal remains contentious. Supporters argue that carbon pricing is necessary to encourage investment in cleaner marine fuels and help meet the IMO’s target of achieving net-zero greenhouse gas emissions from international shipping by or around 2050.

Opponents, including the US and several oil-producing countries, have raised concerns about its impact on shipping costs and wider economies.

The framework could generate an estimated $10 billion to $15 billion annually, with how the revenue is raised and distributed among the key issues still under negotiation.

Further technical negotiations are scheduled for 23–27 November, followed by the IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee meeting from 30 November to 3 December.

The framework is expected to return for possible adoption at an extraordinary session on 4 December.

Trump’s latest intervention signals that Washington intends to maintain its opposition as IMO members move towards the December decision.

text:
With New York Climate Week in full swing, the Global Maritime Forum (GMF) hosted an event showcasing their newly released fifth edition of its “Climate Action in Shipping: Progress towards shipping's 2030 breakthrough”.

According to the GMF, the latest report “reveals mixed progress towards that swiftly approaching target, with multiple indicators demonstrating the flow-on effects of economic and political upheaval, the crisis in Hormuz, energy security and supply chain concerns, and the regulatory uncertainty caused by the failure to adopt the IMO's Net-Zero Framework (NZF) last year.”

The event, held in lower Manhattan at the offices of port and engineering consultants ARUP, featured a panel, moderated by the GMF’s Director of Decarbonization, Jesse Fahnstock, which offered differing viewpoints on the paths towards the GMF year 2030 target of getting to the international side of the industry sourcing 5%, and upwards, of its fuel from “scalable zero-emission sources”. The report is produced jointly by UCL Energy Institute and the Getting to Zero Coalition- tied to the “Marrakech Partnership”- a cooperation framework developed at the 2016 COP conference.

The upcoming IMO MEPC 85 meeting scheduled for late November loomed in the background throughout the GMF event. In the keynote speech prior to the panel discussion, Albon T Ishoda, Marshall Islands’ Ambassador to Fiji and the Pacific Islands, expressed the view that “there remains much to be done,” and voiced that Marshall Islands’ support for a global levy, but recognized that “not all nations are ready for a global levy.” He voices the Marshall Islands’ support for the Net Zero Framework, as it has been proposed. “Global commons problems need global responses,” he said.

The hour-long panel included representatives from AP Moller-Maersk, Mitsui OSK Lines (MOL), and the Panama Canal Authority. Concepcion Boo Arias, Director of Global Partnerships & ESG, Public & Regulatory Affairs, expressed the views that “diversification is the way forward” citing the company’s bet on methanol fueling but pointing to the importance of optionality and flexibility, alluding to the recent announcement of Maersk ordering of 42 LNG-dual fueled vessels.

“We believe in a multi-fuel future,” she added- also mentioning ethanol fuel and a look at onboard carbon capture. She emphasized the need for a global framework, and said that affordability, closing the gap between prices of existing and net zero fuels, is a key concern.

The Panama Canal’s representative, Beatriz Gonzales, talked about the Canal’s initiatives in establishing Green Corridors, and extensive dialogues with fuel suppliers who could bring alternative fuels to transiting vessels.

MOL’s Tatsuro Watanabe also voiced views on the demand issues surrounding the new fuels, and emphasized the need for both short term and long-term actions; “Do what we can do today,” he implored.

In his remarks, he emphasized the extraordinary diversity of the international maritime business, with diverse vessel types traversing different routes across a wide swath of geographies. With this wide variety of ships and trades, he urged all those concerned to respect this diversity of seaborne transit with a diversity of solutions, including wind sails, where an MOL experiment has lowered fuel consumption.

He referred to “technology neutrality- where multiple fuels including some that are not totally completely “green”, would be part of the path forward. Watanabe also noted the multiple layers of participation in seaborne transport and suggested that the cargo side should be “sharing the green premium” with vessel operators.

The GMF, in its summary of findings in the new report, also pointed to last year’s developments at the IMO and this year’s possibilities, saying: “The 2030 target remains achievable, but only if lost momentum is regained quickly through the adoption of the Net-Zero Framework this year, alongside accelerated industry and national action.”

text:
Published: September 24, 2026

NEW YORK – Liberia is lobbying governments to remove the carbon price and global fund from the International Maritime Organization’s net-zero shipping rules before they reconsider adoption. The Liberian team argues that the framework, in its current form, would raise the cost of food, fertilizer, and exports for developing countries that trade with distant markets.

Liberian maritime officials made the case Wednesday at a side event on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly, alongside Foreign Minister Sara Beysolow Nyanti. They presented an alternative co-sponsored by Panama, which the team calls a pragmatic and performance-based path to the IMO’s goal of net-zero emissions from shipping by 2050.

“The issue that we want to address today is not whether we support climate ambition. It is rather whether the IMO proposed measures are fair, practical and connected to real emissions reductions,” said Cllr. Margaret C. Ansumana, deputy commissioner of the Liberia Maritime Authority, who introduced the proposal.

The IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee approved the Net-Zero Framework in April 2025. It would require large ships to meet annual fuel-intensity targets or cover excess emissions with credits bought from other ships or payments into a new IMO Net-Zero Fund. An extraordinary session convened to adopt it in October 2025 instead voted 57 to 49 to adjourn for one year, with 21 abstentions. Reports put adoption later this year, around October or November.

Liberia’s plan would keep a global fuel standard but tie it to fuels that are commercially viable, meaning available, affordable and scalable across all regions, rather than setting it on climate ambition alone. The standard would be reviewed every five years against emissions progress, the impact on developing economies and the maturity of clean fuels.

Ships that beat the standard would earn surplus units they could transfer within a fleet to vessels that fall short. Ships on routes where clean fuel is not available could also earn units for verified energy-efficiency measures, such as slowing down to burn less fuel.

The proposal removes the penalty payments that ships unable to find compliant fuel or surplus units would owe under the current framework. A member of the Liberian technical team, Ms. Grace Nuhn said charging ships for a fuel they cannot get amounts to letting them pay and keep polluting.

“It’s like you’re telling someone that depends on rice to stop eating rice, and the alternative you are providing is not available to them,” said Ms. Nuhn, a technical presenter on the Liberian team. “Rules are made to help people.”

The Liberian team argued that shipowners would not absorb compliance costs and would pass them to consumers. They said countries that import food and fertilizer and export raw materials over long distances would pay the most.

The deputy commissioner Asumana said the framework in its current form is projected to raise about US$10 billion to US$12 billion a year. She called that money a compliance cost that developing economies would ultimately bear, and said it was unclear how much of it would return to them.

A technical officer on the Liberian team said Liberia’s own impact assessment covered only one export, iron ore. The officer said adding rice, the country’s staple, and other goods moved by ship would paint a worse picture. The team urged other least developed countries and small island developing states to run their own country-level assessments rather than rely on regional studies.

The team said the plan would still meet the IMO’s 2023 greenhouse gas strategy. The presenter said it would cut emissions by 25% by 2030, above the strategy’s 20% target, while striving for 30%. By 2040 it would reach about 75%, within the strategy’s range of 70% to 80%, and net zero by 2050, as cleaner fuels mature and the standard tightens.

The Liberian officials also said MARPOL, the international convention on pollution from ships, should remain a technical instrument. They said it should not carry a financing mechanism such as the Net-Zero Fund.

Liberia Maritime Authority Commissioner Neto Zarzar Lighe Sr. said the question for poor and island nations is whether they should first bear heavy trade and economic costs to raise money that may never fully offset the harm.

“Our objective is not to weaken ambition, but to make it achievable, equitable, and sustainable for all member states, especially developing and climate vulnerable countries,” Lighe said.

He described the New York event as a continuation of a presentation the team made in London a few weeks earlier. He thanked Panama for co-sponsoring the proposal.

Minister Nyanti said the Foreign Ministry’s role is to mobilize international support for Liberia’s agenda on maritime safety, maritime security and its net-zero program as part of the country’s climate diplomacy. She said the ministry fully aligns itself with the position of Liberia’s maritime experts. She said discussions on net zero would take place at several high-level meetings and side meetings next month.

Liberia’s Permanent Reprsentative to the United Nations, Amb. Lewis Brown, who closed the event, said Liberia is the largest ship registry by tonnage, which brings climate responsibility. He said Liberia does not want to penalize countries that are not the main polluters, “nor do we wish to permit people who can pay for pollution to simply pay for it and get away with it.”

Several Middle Eastern and North African states supported Liberia’s proposal during IMO talks in April, among them Oman, Kuwait, Jordan, Somalia, Yemen and Tunisia. The president of the Union of Greek Shipowners, Melina Travlos, endorsed it in August.

Liberia, Argentina and Panama had all opposed the framework before sponsoring the alternative. The United States led opposition to the framework when it was presented in 2025.
